# Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem: A Re-examination of the Halden Reduced-Hours Pilot

*Comment, Journal of Labour and Organisation Studies. K. Varga and T. Holm, Centre for Applied Labour Statistics.*

## Abstract

The Halden pilot reported that 61 organisations maintained output while cutting scheduled hours by 20%, implying a 23.4% gain in output per hour. Using the pilot's microdata, released under the Institute's data-sharing policy, we re-examine the result. Four problems, each documented below, account for most of the reported gain: attrition that was not random, a manager-reported output measure that overstates output relative to organisations' own records, an hours denominator that counts scheduled rather than actual time, and an unadjusted revenue comparison. Correcting the first three, the gain in output per hour falls from 23.4% to 10.8% in the subset of organisations where correction is possible. We then argue that the remaining gain is plausibly a novelty effect, and that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty.

## 1. Attrition

The working paper states that nine of the 70 enrolled organisations "withdrew during the preparation phase, chiefly for scheduling reasons". The microdata tell a different story. Seven of the nine withdrew after the reduced schedule had begun: four in the first month and three in the second. In exit forms, six of the nine gave workload or inability to maintain output as the main reason, and two gave scheduling. The organisations that found the change hardest were therefore removed from the sample before the outcome was measured. With nine of 70 organisations missing, and those nine plausibly the least successful, the reported sample of 61 is a sample of survivors.

## 2. The output measure

The primary outcome was an index completed by a manager who was also the pilot's internal sponsor. Managers were asked to base the index on organisational records, but were not required to submit them. Twenty-three organisations did submit underlying records (billable hours delivered, tickets closed, units produced, or cases completed). For these 23 we can compare the manager's index with the index implied by the records.

**Table 1. Manager-reported and record-based output, 23 organisations with records**

| Measure | Mean output index (baseline = 100) |
|---|---|
| Manager-reported index | 98.9 |
| Index computed from submitted records | 95.1 |
| Difference | −3.8 points |

In 19 of the 23 organisations the manager-reported index exceeded the record-based index. We do not suggest bad faith. A manager responsible for a change he or she advocated, asked to rate its effect on a scale where 100 means "unchanged", will tend to round toward success. But the difference is systematic, and the headline output figure of 98.7 should not be taken at face value.

## 3. The hours denominator

The pilot computed output per hour by dividing output by the ratio of scheduled hours, 0.8. Twenty-seven organisations used time-tracking software throughout. Their data show average actual weekly hours of 40.3 at baseline and 34.6 during the pilot, a fall of 14.1% rather than 20%. The difference comes from two sources visible in the logs: longer working days on the remaining four days (average +0.7 hours per day), and work logged on the scheduled day off (on average 1.6 hours per week). Some further work on the day off is probably not logged.

Seventeen organisations have both submitted output records and time tracking. In this subset, record-based output was 95.4 and actual hours fell from 40.4 to 34.8 (−13.9%). The implied gain in output per actual hour is 10.8% (95.4 / 86.1), less than half the reported 23.4%.

**Table 2. Implied gain in output per hour under successive corrections**

| Specification | Output | Hours ratio | Gain per hour |
|---|---|---|---|
| As reported (all 61) | 98.7 | 0.800 | +23.4% |
| Record-based output, scheduled hours (23) | 95.1 | 0.800 | +18.9% |
| Manager-reported output, actual hours (27) | 98.4 | 0.859 | +14.6% |
| Record-based output, actual hours (17) | 95.4 | 0.861 | +10.8% |

## 4. Revenue

The working paper reports revenue 1.4% higher than in the previous year. This is a nominal comparison. Consumer prices rose by 4.1% over the same twelve months; in real terms, revenue in participating organisations fell by approximately 2.6%. Revenue is in any case a poor proxy for productivity, but the figure as presented gives a misleading impression of growth.

## 5. Sectoral claims

The pilot concluded that gains in output per hour were "found in every sector" and that the model is "sector-general". This conclusion is an artifact of the per-hour metric. When hours are cut by 20%, any output index above 80 will register as a per-hour gain. Retail and hospitality output fell by 6.9% on the manager-reported measure; the three retail and hospitality organisations among the 23 with records show a fall of 11.2%. A fall in output of this size in a customer-facing business is not evidence that reduced hours work there. The Varden County trial's counter and contact-centre stratum, the only randomised evidence on coverage-bound work, found a fall in output per employee of 11.4% and longer waits for the public. That is, in our view, the most reliable finding in the literature to date.

## 6. Novelty

After the corrections above, a gain in output per actual hour of about 11% remains in the subset of survivors with usable data. We think this residual should not be read as a durable effect. The pilot's own survey shows self-reported energy at work rising by 0.61 standard deviations at month three and falling to 0.29 at month six. Extrapolating this decline, energy would return to baseline at around month ten. A change that staff chose, welcomed and knew to be under evaluation is the classic setting for a novelty effect: effort rises while the change is new and observed, and falls back once it is routine. Six months is not long enough to distinguish a novelty effect from a durable one, and the burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter.

## 7. The meetings hypothesis

The Varden trial's authors report, in an unregistered exploratory analysis, that cuts in recurring meetings correlated with per-hour gains across seven treated offices, and suggest this as a mechanism. We regard this as a post hoc account fitted to a subgroup. A correlation across seven offices, selected for analysis after the results were known, is precisely the kind of finding that does not replicate. The meetings explanation has an intuitive appeal that has outrun its evidence, and it should not be cited as a mechanism.

## 8. Conclusion

Taking the problems together: attrition removed the organisations least able to cope; the output measure overstated output by roughly four points; the hours measure overstated the reduction in time by roughly six points; and the remaining gain coincides with a decaying measure of enthusiasm. We conclude that the per-hour productivity gains reported for reduced-hours schemes are, in our assessment, entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the best-supported finding is the negative one: where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output.

We recommend that future evaluations use record-based output, actual hours, a randomised or at least matched comparison group, follow-up of at least eighteen months, and analysis of all enrolled organisations including those that withdraw.

## Data note

All re-analyses use the Halden pilot microdata (release 1.2). The corrections in Table 2 can only be computed for subsets of organisations, and those subsets were not chosen at random; organisations with time tracking and records may differ from the others. Our corrected estimates therefore describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole.

response:
# Review of "Hours, Output and the Pilot Problem" (Varga and Holm)

Sections 1–5 are a useful re-analysis. The microdata finding on attrition is new and important, and the output and hours corrections are well done. The headline conclusion is a different matter: the claim that per-hour gains are "entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty" is not supported by the paper's own numbers. It also depends on citing the Varden trial selectively.

Most of the arithmetic checks out:

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| Manager vs record index, 98.9 − 95.1 | −3.8 ✓ |
| 95.1 / 0.8 | +18.9% ✓ |
| 34.6 / 40.3 = 0.859; 98.4 / 0.859 | +14.6% ✓ |
| 34.8 / 40.4 = 0.861; 95.4 / 0.861 | +10.8% ✓ |
| Real revenue, 1.014 / 1.041 | −2.6% ✓ |
| Hours overstatement, 20% vs 14.1% | ≈ 6 points ✓ |

There are two numerical problems, covered in §2 and §5 below.

## 1. The abstract misdescribes what was corrected

The abstract says "Correcting the first three, the gain… falls from 23.4% to 10.8%." The first three problems include attrition, but Table 2 corrects only output and hours. Attrition is never corrected, and the 10.8% figure is still a survivors-only estimate. Either remove attrition from that sentence or add an attrition correction.

An attrition correction is possible. The microdata show that seven of the nine withdrawals happened after the schedule began, so the withdrawn organisations may have one or two months of output data. That allows two things:

- an intention-to-treat estimate that uses whatever data exist for the withdrawn organisations; or
- bounds, by giving the nine organisations pessimistic values, for example zero per-hour gain or the worst observed sector outcome.

With 9 of 70 organisations missing, even a harsh assumption would probably move the overall estimate by only a few points. That is worth showing rather than leaving the reader to assume the bias is large.

## 2. The hours breakdown doesn't add up

Section 3 attributes the gap between scheduled and actual hours to two sources: +0.7 hours a day on the four working days, and 1.6 hours logged on the day off. Together that is 4 × 0.7 + 1.6 = **4.4 hours above the 32-hour schedule**, or about 36.4 hours a week. The reported pilot average is **34.6**, only 2.6 hours above schedule. Measuring the +0.7 from baseline actual days (about 8.06 hours) makes the gap larger, not smaller.

The breakdown may be averaged over different organisations, or the +0.7 may be measured from some other reference. Whatever the reason, it needs reconciling, because it is the evidence offered for the hours correction.

## 3. Record-based output is treated as the true measure

Finding that managers' figures exceeded the records in 19 of 23 organisations is good evidence of upward bias, and the paper presents it fairly. But the records are not automatically closer to true output:

- **"Billable hours delivered" measures hours, not output.** Any organisation that used it will show output falling in proportion to the hours cut, whatever happened to productivity. Report how many of the 23 used billable hours, and show the correction with those organisations excluded.
- **Counts ignore case mix and quality.** Tickets closed and cases completed take no account of difficulty. A manager's overall judgement may be biased and still capture something the counts miss.

The fairest wording is that the two measures differ systematically and the records are probably closer to the truth. The paper instead treats the gap as pure overstatement.

## 4. Revenue

The correction is right in direction, but CPI is a consumer-price index. Revenue for these sectors would be better deflated by output prices for the relevant sectors, which may have risen faster or slower than 4.1%. The conclusion that real revenue did not grow will probably hold. "Approximately 2.6%" implies more precision than the deflator supports.

## 5. The novelty argument is the weakest part, and the conclusion depends on it

After correction, the paper's own estimate is a **+10.8% gain** in output per actual hour. Calling that an artifact requires showing that novelty explains it. Section 6 does not show this:

- **Wrong variable.** The decline is in self-reported energy, not output. No evidence links the energy path to the output path.
- **Two points, and a miscalculation.** Energy fell by 0.32 SD over three months, about 0.107 a month. At that rate the remaining 0.29 reaches zero after about 2.7 more months, at **roughly month 8.7, not month ten**. Fitting a straight line through two survey waves cannot tell decay from levelling off.
- **The paper's own preferred source contradicts it.** This is the decisive point. Section 5 calls the Varden counter stratum "the most reliable finding in the literature," but the comment never mentions the same trial's case-processing stratum. That stratum was:
  - randomised, so survivor bias doesn't apply;
  - measured on administrative output, so manager inflation doesn't apply;
  - measured on actual timesheet hours, so the scheduled-hours denominator doesn't apply;
  - imposed on offices rather than chosen by staff, which weakens the "change staff chose and welcomed" route to novelty;
  - run for nine months, longer than the comment's own extrapolated end of the novelty effect.

  It found **+12.5% per actual hour (95% CI +6.9 to +18.4)**, almost the same as the comment's corrected 10.8%. Each of the comment's three explanations is either ruled out or weakened by that design. Citing Varden's negative stratum as decisive while leaving out its positive stratum is a serious omission.
- **Burden of proof.** "The burden of proof lies with those claiming the latter" is rhetoric. Six months of data cannot show that the gain is durable. They cannot show it is entirely novelty either, and "entirely an artifact" is a claim that needs evidence.

## 6. The meetings section misrepresents the Varden paper

- **Selection.** Varden's meeting data cover all seven treated case-processing offices, collected in month six at managers' request. The offices were not "selected for analysis after the results were known."
- **What Varden claimed.** The authors explicitly said the analysis was unregistered, that seven offices cannot establish a mechanism, and that they had registered a confirmatory test. They did not claim it as a mechanism. "Should not be cited as a mechanism" agrees with them, but the passage reads as if they had made the claim.
- **The randomised comparison is ignored.** Varden reports 3.8 against 7.1 hours of meetings in treated versus control offices. That is a randomised contrast, and stronger evidence than the seven-office correlation the comment criticises.
- A fair criticism the comment misses: Varden has no baseline meeting data. So "offices that cut meetings most" is not something it could measure, only meeting levels at month six.

The right position is that the meetings hypothesis is unconfirmed until the registered test reports, not that it should be dismissed.

## 7. Sectoral claims (Section 5)

- The point that any index above 80 shows a per-hour gain is correct and important.
- The −11.2% retail figure comes from **three organisations** and needs that caveat.
- Lining up the Halden retail figures with Varden's −11.4% compares different things. Halden's index is an organisation's total output against its own baseline. Varden's figure is output per employee against randomised controls, in public counter services, not retail.
- "Where output depends on presence, reduced hours reduce output" overstates Varden's result. Varden held staffing fixed, so its result is that reduced hours *without extra staff* reduce output in coverage-bound work.

## 8. The conclusion contradicts the data note

The data note rightly says the corrected estimates "describe those subsets, not the pilot as a whole." Yet the conclusion extends "entirely an artifact" from the Halden subsets to "reduced-hours schemes" generally. A conclusion that fits the evidence would be something like:

> Correcting for output measurement and actual hours roughly halves the Halden gain, to about 11% in the subset with usable data. Attrition and novelty may account for some of the remainder, but the only randomised evidence (Varden case-processing, nine months) finds a per-hour gain of similar size. Gains appear in work not tied to presence; in coverage-bound work, output per employee falls unless staffing is increased.

## Summary of recommended changes

1. Correct the abstract: attrition is not part of the 10.8% correction. Add attrition bounds or an intention-to-treat estimate.
2. Reconcile the hours breakdown (4.4 hours) with the reported actual hours (2.6 hours above schedule).
3. Report how many record-based organisations measured output as billable hours, and re-run the correction without them.
4. Engage with the Varden case-processing result in Sections 5, 6 and 8.
5. Correct the extrapolation (month ~8.7, not ten), and drop or heavily qualify the novelty inference.
6. Restate the Varden meetings analysis accurately.
7. Replace "entirely an artifact" with a conclusion that matches the corrected estimates and the data note.

Sections 1–4 make a real contribution and would stand on their own. Section 1 in particular shows that the original working paper misreported when and why organisations withdrew, which matters. The overreach in Sections 6–8 is what a referee would object to most.
